description: The two kinds of partner without which PastBook cannot deliver a book: the partner printing facilities on four continents that receive print-ready orders through an API or hot folder, produce hardcover and softcover books, calendars and posters on FSC-certified paper in the country of the customer and hand them to carriers within the published delivery windows; and the platforms and channels PastBook depends on and must comply with, Meta for Facebook Login and photos, Apple's App Store and Google Play, Dropbox and Google Drive, the payment providers behind Visa, Mastercard, American Express and PayPal, and the carriers. Neither owns the consumer relationship, yet both set hard constraints: print partners decide whether the Q4 peak ships on time, and platforms set the rules and can withdraw a channel, as Instagram did when it discontinued third-party access for personal accounts.

customers.name: Print Partner
customers.description: The plant or account manager of a partner printing facility in PastBook's network, in the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil or India, one of the facilities on four continents that produce most orders in the country of the customer and ship to 150+ countries. The facility receives print-ready, imposed PDFs and order data through an order API or a hot folder, produces small 8.5" x 6" and large 12" x 8.5" hardcover books, softcovers, wall calendars and posters on FSC-certified paper, packs them and hands them to the carrier within the production time that starts on payment. It never sees the consumer: PastBook owns the app, the curation, the pricing and the support, and the facility is measured on orders produced within SLA, print defect rate and the capacity it can commit for the Q4 peak when Year in Review books, calendars and gifts have to reach customers before Christmas. It wants steady, error-free volume, an early and honest peak forecast, one clear quality specification, and unit prices and payment terms that make the PastBook line profitable next to its other online print buyers.
careAbout: Print-ready files that run without operator intervention: imposed, preflighted PDFs with the right cover type for the page count (softcover up to 16 pages, hardcover from 27 to 300), correct bleed and colour, and calendar and poster formats that match the machines
Predictable daily volume and an early, honest Q4 forecast, because PastBook's holiday peak is when presses, binding lines and temporary staff are planned months ahead
One SLA and quality specification that defines when a book is late or defective and is applied the same way to every facility in the network
Order data, packing slips and carrier labels that match the job, so a parcel leaves the same day production finishes and is trackable in the country's delivery window
Fair unit prices per book, extra page and product, timely payment for produced volume, and chargebacks only for defects the facility actually caused
FSC paper and local-production requirements that fit the facility's existing certifications and stock, so PastBook's sustainability claims cost no extra qualification effort
winsThem: An order feed with an API or a hot folder, status callbacks and a test environment that a facility integrates in weeks and that carries every job with its files, product specification and packing slip
Routing that sends volume by proximity and committed capacity and grows the facility's share as its SLA and defect performance proves itself
A shared SLA dashboard showing the same on-time, rejection and defect numbers PastBook's production operations manager sees, so reviews start from one set of facts
Weekly Q4 forecasts and capacity reservations agreed in summer, with overflow rules to a second facility instead of a surprise backlog in December
A root-cause dialogue on reprints and quality incidents with one named contact in PastBook production operations, rather than blanket penalties
theirFear: A Q4 surge beyond the forecast that turns into missed Christmas deliveries, refunds and a public argument over whose fault the backlog was
Files that render wrong at the facility, with colour shifts, wrong page counts or a softcover where a hardcover was ordered, so the facility eats the reprint cost
Being routed away quietly as new facilities join the network, losing the volume it staffed and invested for

jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: Run PastBook jobs through the facility as a standard production line: integrate the order feed once, accept and validate each routed job, produce the books, calendars and posters to the agreed specification, pack and hand the parcels to the carrier inside the production time, report status back, and resolve the rare rejected file or reprint without stopping the line.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: Every routed job arrives complete and printable, is produced within the SLA that keeps the country's delivery window (for example 3-5 business days after production in France, the Netherlands, Italy and Germany), leaves with a working tracking number, and the facility's defect and rejection numbers stay low enough that PastBook keeps sending volume.

customerJourneyStories.name: A regional printer joins the PastBook network
customerJourneyStories.summary: The operations director of a digital print facility in Australia with spare capacity on its hardcover binding line is approached by PastBook, which wants to produce Australian orders locally instead of shipping them across the ocean, passes the quality audit, integrates the order feed, starts with a small routing share and grows into the primary facility for the region.

stages.narrative: The facility's presses are under-used outside its own peak, and its board wants online print volume without building a consumer brand or a marketing budget. At the same time PastBook, whose customers after North America are most numerous in Australia, wants to cut a 5-10 business day cross-continent shipment and its emissions by producing in the country of the customer.

PastBook's production operations manager finds the facility through its FSC certification and existing hardcover work for other online brands and asks for a call. The director, in turn, looks up PastBook: 10 million books created since 2012, 1M+ app downloads, a 4.5 Trustpilot score and a partner network already on four continents, so the volume promise is credible.

Both sides evaluate. PastBook orders blind samples of the small and large hardcover, a calendar and a poster, checks colour, binding, spine alignment and FSC stock, and reviews capacity and carrier contracts for the Australian 5-10 day window. The director reviews the SLA and quality specification, the unit price per book and extra page, payment terms, the chargeback rules, and the effort to connect a hot folder versus the API.

A pilot starts with a fixed share of Australian orders routed to the facility through the hot folder, with status callbacks and tracking numbers flowing back. The first weeks surface a product-code mismatch on calendars and a bleed issue on posters, both fixed in the file package, after which acceptance runs without manual checks and the pilot books pass PastBook's quality audit.

Routing share grows as on-time and defect numbers hold, the facility appears on the shared SLA dashboard next to the network average, and weekly forecasts arrive with the Q4 curve for Year in Review books and calendars. In summer the director commits peak capacity per week and agrees the overflow point at which PastBook reroutes to another facility.

The facility stays because the volume is steady, arrives print-ready and pays on time, and because it became the primary facility for Australia and New Zealand within two seasons; the director invests in a second binding line for the next Q4 on the strength of the shared forecast. PastBook keeps it because Australian customers now get books within the published window from a local plant.

customerJourneyStories.name: An EU partner becomes redundant peak capacity for a second region
customerJourneyStories.summary: The account manager of an established German partner that already produces PastBook's German, Dutch, French and Italian orders is asked to take Q4 overflow for the rest of the EU and, when the UK facility saturates, for UK orders, turning a single-region supplier into the network's redundant capacity for Europe.

stages.narrative: In the previous December a single European facility ran out of capacity, late Christmas deliveries produced refunds and one-star reviews that PastBook's support had to answer within 48 hours, and the production operations manager was told to have redundant capacity per region before the next peak.

At the quarterly partner review PastBook proposes that the German facility, which has the best on-time and defect record in the network, becomes the overflow destination for other European orders during Q4. The account manager had not considered cross-border volume because the facility's own contracts are domestic.

The account manager works through what changes: delivery windows for the rest of the EU (5-7 business days after production) versus the domestic 3-5, carrier rates for cross-border parcels, packaging and language of the packing slip, extra staffing for a few weeks, and a price for overflow volume that is not guaranteed. PastBook shows the routing rules, the forecast that triggers overflow and the SLA that will be measured.

During the first Q4 week the overflow rule fires: a share of orders from the rest of the EU and, for two days, from the UK is routed to the facility. Tracking numbers and status callbacks work unchanged, the cross-border parcels arrive inside the published windows, and the facility reports the extra volume on the shared dashboard without an incident.

Overflow becomes a standing arrangement: capacity reserved per Q4 week for a second region, joint review of the forecast accuracy after each season, and a small year-round share of rest-of-EU orders so the cross-border process never goes cold. The facility's account manager now attends PastBook's pre-season planning call in summer.

The facility keeps the role because the peak weeks are its most profitable of the year and the forecast makes them plannable; PastBook keeps it because Europe now has redundant capacity and no December depends on a single plant. When PastBook adds a new EU facility, the German partner's overflow role is written into the routing rules rather than eroded.

top.name: Orders produced within SLA
top.description: Share of routed jobs that leave production at the partner facility within the agreed production time, weighted across the network's facilities on four continents; the Q4 peak pulls the yearly figure down. Modeled seed value for a network producing most orders in the customer's country, not an official PastBook figure.

branches.name: Production readiness of incoming orders
branches.description: Whether the jobs a facility receives are complete and printable and whether the order feed behaves reliably, so capacity is spent on production rather than on fixing input.

children.name: Print file rejection rate
children.description: Share of routed jobs the facility rejects or holds because the file, page count, cover type or order data would fail on press.

children.name: Preflight pass rate before routing
children.description: Share of print-ready files that pass PastBook's own preflight (imposition, bleed, resolution, page-count versus cover rules) at the first attempt before they are routed.

children.name: Order data errors per 1,000 jobs
children.description: Jobs per 1,000 in which address, quantity, product code or packing slip did not match the file package.

children.name: Jobs acknowledged within 15 minutes
children.description: Share of routed jobs the facility's system acknowledges through the API or hot folder within 15 minutes, the signal that the feed and the facility are both live.

children.name: Order feed integration uptime
children.description: Availability of the partner order API, hot folder transfer and callback endpoints as seen by the facility.

children.name: Status callback completeness
children.description: Share of jobs with the full set of status events (received, in production, shipped with tracking) reported back to PastBook.

branches.name: Production and handover performance
branches.description: How the facility performs once a job is accepted: capacity in the peak, defects, and how fast finished parcels reach the carrier.

children.name: Peak capacity utilisation
children.description: Share of the capacity the facility committed for the busiest Q4 week that is actually used; above about 90 percent late jobs rise, so the target leaves headroom.

children.name: Forecast accuracy of Q4 volume shared by PastBook
children.description: Share of Q4 weeks in which actual routed volume was within 10 percent of the forecast PastBook shared with the facility.

children.name: Overflow jobs rerouted in peak
children.description: Share of Q4 jobs first routed to the facility that had to be rerouted to another facility because committed capacity was exhausted.

children.name: Print defect rate
children.description: Share of produced books, calendars and posters found defective in the facility's quality control or in customer complaints attributed to production.

children.name: Reprints attributed to the facility per 1,000 books
children.description: Reprint cases per 1,000 books whose root cause was production at the facility (binding, colour, trimming, page order) rather than the file or transport.

children.name: Same-day carrier handover rate
children.description: Share of parcels handed to the carrier on the day production of the order was completed.

top.name: Gross margin after print and shipping cost
top.description: PastBook's gross margin on printed products after the partner's production cost and the shipping cost, as a share of net product revenue; the margin between retail price (small hardcover USD 19.99, large USD 34.99 for 24 pages) and partner cost is what the print network protects. Modeled seed value, not an official PastBook figure.

branches.name: Production and shipping cost per order
branches.description: What a produced and shipped order costs PastBook at the partner, driven by unit price, waste, local production and consolidation.

children.name: Unit production cost per book
children.description: Average partner price paid per produced book across small and large hardcover and softcover, including extra pages and FSC paper.

children.name: Production cost per extra page
children.description: Partner cost per page beyond the 24-page base, against the USD 0.40 (small) and USD 0.55 (large) retail price per extra page.

children.name: Waste and spoilage rate in production
children.description: Share of printed sheets and covers discarded at the facility during production of PastBook jobs.

children.name: Shipping cost per order
children.description: Average carrier cost per shipped order from the facility to the customer, including cross-border parcels.

children.name: Orders produced in the customer's country
children.description: Share of orders produced by a facility in the same country as the delivery address, which cuts shipping cost, transit days and emissions.

children.name: Multi-product orders consolidated in one parcel
children.description: Share of orders with more than one product (for example a book and a calendar) shipped as a single parcel on the longest production time.

branches.name: Network resilience and failure cost
branches.description: Whether the network can absorb a peak or a facility outage per region and what production and delivery failures cost PastBook.

children.name: Regions with redundant partner capacity
children.description: Delivery regions (US, Canada, UK, EU, Australia and New Zealand, Brazil, India) that have at least two facilities able to produce the full product range within the published window.

children.name: Active partner facilities
children.description: Facilities with a live integration and at least one routed job in the last quarter.

children.name: Share of volume at the largest single facility
children.description: Share of yearly orders produced by the single largest facility in the network, a concentration measure.

children.name: Reprint and refund cost as share of revenue
children.description: Cost of reprints, replacement shipping and refunds caused by production or delivery failures, as a share of net product revenue.

children.name: Reprints charged back to the partner
children.description: Share of facility-attributable reprint cost recovered from the partner under the SLA chargeback rules.

children.name: Late-delivery refunds in peak season
children.description: Refunds per 1,000 Q4 orders granted because the parcel missed the published delivery window before the occasion.

customers.name: Platform and Channel Partner
customers.description: The partner, developer-relations or policy contact at one of the platforms PastBook depends on and must comply with: Meta for Facebook Login and the photo permissions behind Facebook Photo Books, Apple's App Store and Google Play for app review, featuring, privacy labels and billing rules, Dropbox and Google Drive for cloud imports, the payment providers behind Visa, Mastercard, American Express and PayPal in seven currencies, and the carriers that deliver to 150+ countries. The platform sets the rules, and PastBook lives within them: it has 1M+ app downloads, was featured by the App Store in several countries in September 2022, and lost its Instagram import when Instagram discontinued third-party access for personal accounts, which is why the phone camera roll and Facebook are now the primary sources. The platform wants a developer that passes review, uses personal photos only for the customer's own book and deletes them on request, keeps chargebacks and complaints low, adopts API changes on time, and brings volume that makes the relationship worth a named contact.
careAbout: An app that respects the platform's guidelines at every release: clear purpose strings for photo-library access, accurate privacy labels, account and data deletion, no misleading promotions

Data use that stays within the permission granted: Facebook albums, timeline pictures and profile photos used only to build that customer's book, imported over encrypted connections and deleted on request, never retained beyond the order
Low burden on the platform's own support: few payment disputes and chargebacks, few user complaints about photo access, no policy escalations
Quality that reflects well on the store or platform: crash-free releases, a 4.5-plus rating, seasonal content worth featuring around Year in Review and Mother's Day
Timely adoption of new SDK versions, API deprecations and payment scheme rules with a clean migration, not a last-minute exception request
Volume that matters: installs, transactions and parcels that make PastBook a developer or merchant the platform assigns a named contact to
winsThem: A developer with 10 million books created, 1M+ app downloads and a 4.5 Trustpilot score that has passed App Store and Google Play review for years and answers a reviewer's question within a day
A documented privacy programme (encrypted transfer and storage, GDPR and CCPA rights, consent and deletion tooling) that makes Meta's data-use review and the store privacy labels straightforward
An integration gateway that isolates the Meta Graph API, Dropbox, Google Drive, payment providers, carriers and store APIs, so a deprecation is a contained migration rather than an outage
Featuring-ready seasonal releases and store pages in ten languages timed with the platform's editorial calendar, as in the September 2022 App Store feature in several countries
Clean payments: recognisable order descriptors, low chargeback rates and refunds handled by PastBook's 24/7 support before a dispute reaches the provider
theirFear: A developer mishandling users' photos of children, faces and locations and the resulting privacy incident being reported as the platform's failure
A policy change, like the one that ended Instagram's third-party access, breaking a popular use case and sending angry users to the platform rather than to the developer
A Q4 peak of transactions and parcels bringing fraud, chargebacks and delivery disputes that the platform has to arbitrate

jobsToBeDone.name: Keep the app and integrations compliant with platform policies
jobsToBeDone.whatItIs: Keep a developer that reaches millions of users' photos inside the rules: publish the requirements, review the app and its permission requests at each release, verify how Facebook, camera roll and cloud photos are used and deleted, watch integration health and abuse signals such as failed logins, rate limits and payment fraud, and manage policy changes and deprecations with a migration window the developer can meet.
jobsToBeDone.outcome: PastBook passes app review and data-use checks first time, its permissions match what the book flow needs, personal photos are deleted on request and never kept beyond the order, integrations stay healthy through SDK and API changes, and the platform records no policy incident against the developer in a year.

jobsToBeDone.outcome: Orders originating through the platform's channel grow year on year, with installs converting to orders, logins and payments succeeding, parcels arriving inside the published windows and the developer's rating and complaint numbers staying good enough for the platform to keep featuring and trusting it.

streamsNeeded.howItSupports: Aligns Year in Review and holiday releases with the platform's editorial and campaign calendar.

customerJourneyStories.name: App Store: from first review to featured in several countries
customerJourneyStories.summary: Apple's app review and editorial side meets PastBook when the AI-driven 1-click photo book app is submitted in 2021, reviews its photo-library access and privacy labels release after release, and by September 2022 features it in several countries; the relationship holds because the app keeps passing review and keeps its rating.

stages.narrative: A new photo-product app that asks for full photo-library access and sells physical books outside in-app purchase is submitted for review in July 2021. For the platform this is a category with real privacy stakes, children's photos and family moments, so the developer has to prove that access is justified and data use is transparent.

The reviewers see the app among many photo-book apps; what makes it stand out is the claim of a finished book in under 60 seconds from the camera roll, a company that already had 10 million books behind it and a Trustpilot score of 4.5, and a first build whose purpose strings and privacy label described exactly what the app did.

Each release is checked against the guidelines: the reason for photo-library access, the privacy label against actual data flows, physical goods paid by card or PayPal rather than in-app purchase, account deletion inside the app, and store text in ten languages that matches the product. Two early builds are sent back for a label mismatch and a missing deletion path, both fixed within days.

The first approved releases go live in the US, then in other storefronts; installs grow and the store sees the ratings and crash reports that follow. Editorial notices the seasonal Year in Review release and tests the app against its featuring bar: quality, localisation, a story worth telling about turning a year of photos into a book.

By September 2022 the App Store features PastBook in several countries; in July 2023 the highlight video sharing release passes review and gives the store another story to tell. Releases now pass first time, the developer responds within a day to reviewer questions, and the platform contact expects the Q4 build in early autumn.

The platform keeps featuring and ranking the app because it stays at 1M+ downloads with a high rating, low crash and complaint rates and clean privacy labels through every new requirement; PastBook keeps its place by treating each guideline change as a planned release. When the store introduces a new privacy or deletion rule, PastBook is among the developers already compliant, and its seasonal releases are pencilled into the editorial calendar.

customerJourneyStories.name: Meta: keeping Facebook Photo Books running after the Instagram withdrawal
customerJourneyStories.summary: Meta's platform team sees PastBook first as one of many apps using Instagram photos and then, after Instagram discontinues third-party access for personal accounts, as a developer whose Facebook Photo Books flow for the years 2009 to 2025 depends on Facebook Login and photo permissions and must pass data-use review every year.

stages.narrative: Instagram shifts its focus and discontinues support for third-party tools for personal accounts. For PastBook this ends a core import channel overnight; for Meta it means a wave of developers asking how to keep serving users who want their social-media photos printed, and PastBook's Facebook flow becomes the developer's remaining Meta channel.

Meta's platform team sees an app requesting Facebook photo permissions at scale that builds one book per year from albums, timeline pictures, cover and profile photos and mobile uploads with captions, publishes a clear statement to its users about the Instagram change, and points them to Facebook, the phone app and manual upload rather than to a workaround.

The permission request is reviewed: does the year-book flow need each permission, is the privacy policy accurate, is business verification complete, does the app implement data deletion so a user's photos are removed on request and not kept beyond the order, and are photos transferred over encrypted connections. PastBook's privacy and consent tooling answers each question with documentation rather than promises.

Permissions are granted at production scale and the Facebook Photo Books flow runs through its first holiday season under Meta's terms: import completion is monitored, deletion requests are executed and logged, and no data-use complaint reaches the platform from the thousands of year-books made in the peak.

The relationship settles into an annual rhythm: the data-use review is completed on time each year with the same documentation, SDK and Graph API version changes are adopted inside the deprecation window through PastBook's integration gateway, and Meta's contact hears from PastBook before a change ships rather than after something breaks.

Meta keeps the developer because it has had no policy incident in years and gives Facebook users a reason to value their photo archive; PastBook stays because the Facebook flow is the only way its timeline archivists can print 2009 to 2025 in one click, while it deliberately grows the phone and cloud-drive sources so that a second withdrawal would never again cost it a core channel.

productStrategy.vision: Be the developer and merchant every platform wants in its ecosystem: an app that passes review first time, a privacy programme that treats users' photos as the platform would, payments and parcels that create no disputes, and a customer relationship owned through the PastBook app and account, so that growth through Meta, the App Store, Google Play, cloud drives, payment providers and carriers is never again hostage to a single policy decision like Instagram's withdrawal.
